different subtypes (subgroup and EPEC lineage) of potentially pathogenic Escherichia (E.) coli strains dominate in different geographical areas.
different subtypes dominate the infant gut microbiota in different geographical areas, and these subtypes are associated with different virulence characteristics.
the B2 subtypes that dominate the gut microbiota are different in Swedish and Pakistani infants, and that the ExPEC virulence factors are more prevalent in Swedish infants.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the E. coli strains in the gut microbiotas of Swedish and Pakistani infants and their pathogenic potential.
how the intestinal microbiota of infants is colonized with E. coli strains and how the strains are related to the strains that cause infections.
the role of the infant gut microbiota as a reservoir for E. coli strains with different pathogenic potential.

the B2 subtypes of E. coli that colonize the gut of infants are not only different in their geographical origin and prevalence, but they also differ in the presence or absence of ExPEC traits, and the EPEC traits are also different between the two groups.

E. coli strains of different phylogenetic subtypes dominate the intestinal microbiota of infants from different geographical areas and that different E. coli subtypes have different virulence characteristics, which is in agreement with our previous studies.
the gut microbiota contains different subtypes of E. coli, and the subtypes vary between infants living in different geographic areas.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the E. coli B1 and B2 subgroups are the dominant E. coli subgroups in the gut microbiomes of both Pakistani and Swedish infants.
the E. coli B subgroups that are most common in the gut of Swedish and Pakistani infants are different.
the intestinal B2 E. coli strains from Western populations are more likely to be ExPEC than EPEC strains, whereas EPEC lineages dominate the B2 strains in infants from a developing country.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the gut microbiota contains a large diversity of potentially pathogenic bacteria, which is a risk for the development of infectious diseases.

different subtypes dominate the gut microbiota in infants in different geographical regions and that the ability to cause infections is not necessarily linked to the presence of specific virulence genes but rather to the presence of the entire set of genes that are characteristic of a specific subgroup.
